newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU still long way from tax accord.
newsitem.headline: EU still long way from tax accord.

text.p: The European Union is nowhere near reaching an agreement on avoiding harmful tax competition between its member states despite intense work carried out since the beginning of the year by top finance ministry officials.

Luxembourg's Budget Minister Marc Fischbach told Reuters a large majority of EU countries had asked the European Commission to redraft a proposal for a code of conduct on taxation arguing that it left out a number of related issues.
Concerned that the Commission may try to force through at a later stage binding rules on the taxation of capital income, Fischbach said the code should also look at the taxation of individuals.
More emphasis should also be placed on subsidies paid to attract businesses to certain regions to the detriment of others.
"We need a global package which is sufficiently balanced to be acceptable by all," Fischbach said.

"By global package we mean taking into account direct taxation...We cannot discuss only, as the Commission does, the taxation of companies, we must also discuss taxation of individuals, for example the special regimes for expatriates," Fischbach said in a telephone interview.

Luxembourg has often been accused of distorting competition by attracting the savings of neighbouring Belgians and Germans. It is now worried that a code of conduct will only be a prelude to an EU-wide withholding tax on capital income, an idea dear to the EU commissioner in charge of taxation policy, Mario Monti.
"What Luxembourg is saying is that it would be unfair to have a voluntary code only on corporate tax and then be faced with a draft directive on taxation of capital income," one EU source said.
There is an increasing awarenesss in Europe that different national tax regimes and public grants to businesses are harming fair competition.

The creation of the single currency in 1999, which by removing the exchange rate risk will further encourage the investment of savings in lower tax zones, and the brutal closure of Renault's Belgian plant have highlighted such problems.

But as the Commission, at the request of notably Belgium, Germany and France, seeks agreement on a voluntary code of conduct, which in the first instance would mainly prevent the situation getting worst, most EU states are reluctant to commit themselves.

Ireland, which has also been criticised for its favourable taxation of the manufacturing industry, has also called for a broadening of the debate to offshore zones such as the Channel Islands, EU sources said.

The EU has in the past systematically failed to coordinate the taxation of businesses or capital income tax because fiscal issues require the unanimous consent of all 15 states -- hence the proposal for a code of conduct.

A group of high representatives of finance ministers asked the Commission at their last meeting on Friday to revise its proposal on the code of conduct. This is expected to happen in time for the informal meeting of EU finance ministers on September 12 to 14 which will discuss the issue.
